entries.explanation: WCAG requires body text to hit a 4.5:1 contrast ratio so it stays readable without assistive technology.
entries.title: Text doesn't have enough contrast with its background
entries.userImpact: People with low vision or color blindness may be unable to read the text at all. It also affects anyone on a dim screen or in bright sunlight.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the color-contrast rule passes.
Measure the ratio with a contrast checker (4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text).
Zoom to 200% and confirm the text is still readable.

entries.explanation: Every meaningful image needs alt text; purely decorative images should have an empty alt so assistive technology skips them.
entries.title: Image has no text alternative
entries.userImpact: Screen reader users hear only 'image' or the file name, so any information in the picture is lost to them.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the image-alt rule passes.
With a screen reader on, confirm the image is announced meaningfully.
If the image is decorative, use alt="" and confirm it is skipped.

entries.explanation: Link text should describe the destination on its own, since screen reader users often navigate link-by-link out of context.

fix.before: click here to read the full report.

entries.title: Link has no discernible text
entries.userImpact: A link that just says 'click here' tells a screen reader user nothing about where it goes, forcing them to hunt through surrounding text to guess.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the link-name rule passes.
Tab through the page and confirm each link's purpose is clear from its text alone.

entries.explanation: Every button needs an accessible name — visible text, or an aria-label for icon-only buttons (with the icon hidden from assistive tech).

fix.after:
<button onclick="closeModal()" aria-label="Close dialog">
  <svg aria-hidden="true"><!-- X icon --></svg>
</button>

entries.title: Button has no discernible text
entries.userImpact: Screen readers announce the control as just 'button', so users have no idea what activating it does. Icon-only buttons are the usual culprit.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the button-name rule passes.
With a screen reader, confirm it is announced as 'Close dialog, button'.

entries.explanation: The <title> is the first thing screen readers announce and what shows in tabs and bookmarks — it should describe the page.
entries.title: Page has no title or the title is empty
entries.userImpact: Without a meaningful title, users can't tell which page they've landed on, especially with several tabs open.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the document-title rule passes.
Open the page and confirm the tab shows a descriptive title.

entries.explanation: The lang attribute tells assistive technology which language profile to use for pronunciation.
entries.title: <html> element is missing a lang attribute
entries.userImpact: Screen readers may read the page with the wrong language's pronunciation rules, making it hard to understand.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the html-has-lang rule passes.
Confirm the value matches the page's primary language.

entries.explanation: Inputs need a visible, programmatically associated <label>. Placeholder text is not a label — it disappears on input and isn't reliably announced.
entries.title: Form input has no associated label
entries.userImpact: Screen reader users can't tell what a field is for, and sighted users lose the bigger click target a label provides.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the label rule passes.
Click each label and confirm focus moves to its input.
With a screen reader, confirm each field is announced with its label.

entries.explanation: A <main> landmark lets assistive technology jump straight to the primary content. (axe flags this as best practice; closest WCAG criterion is 1.3.1.)
entries.title: Page has no main landmark
entries.userImpact: Screen reader and keyboard users must tab through the header and navigation on every page load instead of skipping to the content.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the landmark rules pass.
With a screen reader, confirm you can jump directly to the main landmark.

entries.explanation: All content should live inside landmarks (header, nav, main, footer) so it shows up in landmark navigation. (axe best practice; closest WCAG criterion is 1.3.1.)
entries.title: Page content isn't contained in landmarks
entries.userImpact: Content outside landmarks is invisible to landmark navigation, so screen reader users can miss it entirely.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the region rule passes.
Use a screen reader's landmark list and confirm every content block appears.

entries.explanation: Headings should descend one level at a time (h1 → h2 → h3). Skipping levels breaks the document outline that assistive tech builds. (axe best practice; closest WCAG criterion is 1.3.1.)
entries.title: Heading levels are skipped
entries.userImpact: Screen reader users navigate by headings; skipped levels make the page structure confusing and hard to skim.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the heading-order rule passes.
Check the heading outline reads as a sensible hierarchy.

entries.explanation: IDs must be unique — duplicates break label associations, ARIA references, and any script that looks elements up by id.
entries.title: The same id is used on multiple elements
entries.userImpact: A label or aria-describedby pointing at a duplicated id may resolve to the wrong element, so screen readers announce the wrong information.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the duplicate-id rule passes.
Search the markup for any remaining duplicate ids.

entries.explanation: Each ARIA role supports only specific attributes; using a disallowed one means assistive technology will ignore it.
entries.title: ARIA attribute isn't allowed on this element
entries.userImpact: The intended information never reaches screen reader users — the attribute is silently dropped.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the aria-allowed-attr rule passes.
Confirm the chosen role actually supports the attribute (check the ARIA spec).

entries.explanation: Some roles require specific child roles (e.g. list needs listitem, tablist needs tab). Without them the structure is incomplete.
entries.title: ARIA parent is missing its required children
entries.userImpact: Screen readers may not expose the widget's structure at all, leaving users unable to perceive or operate it.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the aria-required-children rule passes.
Confirm every required child role is present.

entries.explanation: <ul> and <ol> may only directly contain <li> (plus script/template). Anything else breaks list semantics.
entries.title: List contains elements that aren't list items
entries.userImpact: Screen readers announce list structure ('list, 3 items'); stray elements confuse the count and the navigation.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the list rule passes.
Confirm the list contains only li elements.

entries.explanation: <li> elements must be contained in a <ul>, <ol>, or an element with role=list.
entries.title: List item isn't inside a list
entries.userImpact: An orphaned list item loses its list context, so screen readers can't announce position ('2 of 5').
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the listitem rule passes.
Confirm every li sits inside a ul, ol, or role=list.

entries.explanation: The viewport must not set maximum-scale below 2 or user-scalable=no — users need to be able to zoom.
entries.title: Viewport meta tag disables zooming
entries.userImpact: People with low vision who rely on pinch-zoom are locked out of enlarging the content.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the meta-viewport rule passes.
On a mobile device, confirm pinch-zoom works.

entries.explanation: Pages need a skip link, landmarks, or headings so keyboard users can bypass repeated blocks like navigation.

fix.after:
Skip to main content
...

entries.title: No way to skip repeated content
entries.userImpact: Keyboard-only users have to tab through the entire nav on every single page before reaching the content.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the bypass rule passes.
Tab from the top of the page and confirm the skip link appears and works.

entries.explanation: <iframe> elements need a title describing their content so users know what the embedded region is.
entries.title: Frame has no title
entries.userImpact: Screen reader users encounter an unnamed frame and can't tell whether it's worth entering or should be skipped.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the frame-title rule passes.
With a screen reader, confirm the frame is announced with its title.

entries.explanation: SVGs acting as images need a <title> child or role=img with an aria-label so assistive technology can name them.

fix.after:
<svg role="img" aria-label="Revenue trend chart, rising">
  <!-- chart -->
</svg>

entries.title: SVG image has no accessible name
entries.userImpact: Without a name, the graphic is announced as an unlabeled image and its meaning is lost.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the svg-img-alt rule passes.
With a screen reader, confirm the graphic is announced with its name.

entries.explanation: <input type="image"> is a submit button and needs alt text describing its action.
entries.title: Image button has no text alternative
entries.userImpact: Screen reader users hear only 'button' with no indication of what submitting it does.
verify: Re-run the axe check and confirm the input-button-name rule passes.
With a screen reader, confirm the button's purpose is announced.

note: Curated knowledge base of common axe-core rules. In production this would be a vector-retrieval (RAG) layer over the WCAG spec and internal guidance; here it's a simple lookup by rule id with a generic fallback.
